section: Etymological Explanation of Given Name Provided by the Talmud
note:
ראו אורנשטיין, עמ' 1461\. מניח שם שבגלל שיש אטימולוגיה, חייבים לומר ש"אינו אלא פסבדונים וכנוי לשבח" (\!)  
It is likely that the Talmud was prompted in this, since the name Meir is unusual. In fact, no other Sage has this name.

תענית דף כ ע"א: "תנא לא נקדימון שמו אלא בוני שמו ולמה נקרא שמו נקדימון ש\[...\]"  
It is likely that the Talmud found the Greek name Nakdimon to be unusual to prompt this.

Bavli: [Taanit 25a:7](sefaria:Taanit.25a.7) (1 segments). Gazetteer: “Ikku”. A neighbour of Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa: 'מה שמך? אמרה ליה איכו. אמר: איכו נימטו כשוריך' – he plays on her name (‘may your beams reach’). The Word Play list has only המנונא and לכלוכית.

"זקן אחד" \- אורנשטיין, ערך "זקן אחד", עמ' 972 ואילך.   
"חסיד אחד" \- אורנשטיין, עמ' 1151\. ראו שם ציטוט מהתלמוד: "כל היכא דמאמרינן מעשה בחסיד אחד, או ר' יהודה בן בבא או ר' יהודה בר' עילאי."  
The phrase משום זקן אחד [appears seven times in the Talmud](https://www.sefaria.org/search?q=%D7%9E%D7%A9%D7%95%D7%9D%20%D7%96%D7%A7%D7%9F%20%D7%90%D7%97%D7%93&tab=text&tpathFilters=Talmud&tvar=0&tsort=relevance&svar=1&ssort=relevance).  
In [Berakhot.55b.16](sefaria:Berakhot.55b.16), the Elder is identified as R’ Bana’ah:  
אמר רבי ביזנא בר זבדא, אמר רבי עקיבא, אמר רבי פנדא, אמר רב נחום, אמר רבי בירים, משום זקן אחד, ומנו — רבי בנאה \[...\]  
That statement is also highly unusual for having six \[\!\] tradents cited in chain, instead of the usual two or three. Four of the names are highly unusual: R’ Bizna bar Zavda, R’ Panda, Rav Nahum, and R’ Biriyim.  
In [Chullin.98a.9](sefaria:Chullin.98a.9), the Elder is identified as R’ Ya’akov:  
אמר רב שמן בר אבא, אמר רב אידי בר אידי בר גרשם, אמר לוי בר פרטא, אמר רבי נחום, אמר רבי ביריים, משום זקן אחד \-- ורבי יעקב שמיה, דבי נשיאה אמרו \[...\]  
Here, seven (\!) tradents are cited in the chain, and again we have the exact same chain of Rav Nahum citing R’ Biriyim citing the Elder. It is likely that the Elder is identified by the gloss of the anonymous Talmud as R’ Ya’akov, because R’ Ya’akov was a member of the Nasi’s household.  
In [Bava\_Kamma.82a.2](sefaria:Bava_Kamma.82a.2), the Elder is identified as R’ Yehoshua ben Levi:  
ר' תנחום ור' ברייס אמרי משום זקן אחד, ומנו \-- ר' יהושע בן לוי  
This sugya is the only time that R’ Berayes appears in the Talmud; he’s cited again later in that sugya in the same format, [Bava\_Kamma.81a.9](sefaria:Bava_Kamma.81a.9):  
ר' תנחום ור' ברייס משום זקן אחד

This is the common construct of family name in the Bible.   
On the formula of of “b’nei X” for a family or clan, compare [Banu (Arabic) \- Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banu_\(Arabic\)):  
Banu (بنو) is Arabic for "the children of" or "descendants of" and appears before the name of a tribal progenitor. The English counterpart would be "House of", for example the House of Saud. Another example of the usage is the Bani Quraish, the tribe from which Muhammad came, for which a Quranic Surah is also named \[...\] For example, "Bani Kaab" literally means the sons of Kaab: the house of Kaab.

אורנשטיין, עמ' 2269 ואילך.   
On *rabbi* vs. *rav*, see Norman Solomon, *Talmud,* in his introduction:   
“Sherira claimed that the Talmud applies the title ‘Rabbi’ to scholars in the Land of Israel and ‘Rav’ to Babylonians, and in a letter to the community of Kairouan he wrote, ‘Rabbi is greater than Rav, Rabban is greater than Rabbi, the untitled name is greater than Rabban.’   
Yochanan Breuer has disputed this traditional analysis, arguing that *Rav* was originally a dialectical variant of *Rabbi*, consistent with the Eastern Aramaic habit of dropping possessive endings; *Rabban* (as is generally agreed) was a title reserved for the Nasi, and the ‘untitled name’ by which Hillel and Shammai, for instance, are known is because they predated the use of titles.”

"דהא כי אתא רב הושעיא מנהרדעא, אתא ואייתי מתניתא בידיה: \[...\]"  
This full phrase appears [four times in the Talmud](https://www.sefaria.org/search?q=%D7%A8%D7%91%20%D7%94%D7%95%D7%A9%D7%A2%D7%99%D7%90%20%D7%9E%D7%A0%D7%94%D7%A8%D7%93%D7%A2%D7%90&tab=text&tpathFilters=Talmud&tvar=1&tsort=relevance&svar=1&ssort=relevance).  
This could be read as “When Rav Hoshaya came from Neharde’a \[...\]”. But the phrase כי אתא פלוני always means “When X came \[from Eretz Yisrael\]”, as far as I can tell. Therefore, it seems most reasonable that מנהרדעא is a toponymic surname of Rav Hoshaya.

פסחים קיד ע"א: "רבי יצחק בן אחא דשמעתא הוא רבי יצחק בן פנחס דאגדתא וסימניך (שמעו נא אחיי ורעיי)". ורש"י שם: רבי יצחק ב"ר אחא דשמעתא \- רבי יצחק סתם האמור באגדתא ר' יצחק בן פנחס הוא: שמעו נא אחיי \- דשמעתא בן אחא:  
R’ Yohanan is called the nickname “*bar Nafha”* in a number of places*,* see Levin, p. 56:   
רבי יוחנן נתכנה "בר נפחא" \[...\] ברש"י לסנהדרין צו ע"א: "נראה למורי דאביו של ר' יוחנן הוי נפחא ולהכי מיקרי 'בר נפחא', ואית דמפרשי 'בר נפחא' על שם יופיו".

ראו מרגליות, "לחקר", עמ' 1, על לוי סריסא (הדגשות שלו): "ר׳ לוי **סריסא** המוזכר בירושלמי ביצה פ״ב ה״ה \[...\] שנקרא לוי **סריסא** על שהמשיל **בסריס**.".  
But it seems more likely that this person named Levi was given the epithet סריסא, because he was impotent (=סריס). And the answer referenced an impotent person, because Levi was one. In any case, Marguliyot there, p. 7, argues that Chajes is misreading, and סריסא is not part of the name at all.

On its face it would seem surprising that there are rabbis with the patronym “Titus”. Since the name became strongly associated with the famous Roman emperor Titus, including in the Talmud itself. However, taking into account the general the popularity of the name, both before and after the emperor, this is less surprising. Cf. [Titus (praenomen) \- Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titus_\(praenomen\)): “Titus \[...\] is a Latin praenomen, or personal name, and was one of the most common names throughout Roman history. For most of Roman history, Titus was the sixth most common praenomen, following Lucius, Gaius, Marcus, Publius, and Quintus. While not used by every family, it was widely used by all social classes including both patricians and plebeians and was a favorite of many families and gave rise to the patronymic gens Titia. It was regularly abbreviated T.”
